title: PolicyPilot RAGAS Benchmark (10 Policy Questions)

questions.question: What was the average headline CPI inflation rate for 2023-24 and what factors drove its movement according to the RBI Annual Report?
contexts: Headline CPI inflation moderated to an average of 5.4 per cent in 2023-24 from 6.7 per cent in 2022-23. The easing was primarily driven by a substantial softening in core inflation (CPI excluding food and fuel) to 4.3 per cent, reflecting the impact of monetary policy tightening and easing global supply chain pressures. However, food inflation remained elevated and volatile, registering repeated supply shocks due to erratic weather patterns.
questions.ground_truth: Headline CPI inflation moderated to an average of 5.4 per cent in 2023-24 from 6.7 per cent in 2022-23. The disinflation was driven by core inflation easing to 4.3 per cent due to monetary policy actions, while food inflation remained volatile due to weather shocks.
questions.policypilot_answer: Headline CPI inflation moderated to an average of 5.4 per cent in 2023-24 from 6.7 per cent in 2022-23 [S1]. The decline was primarily driven by a softening in core inflation (CPI excluding food and fuel) to 4.3 per cent [S1]. However, food inflation remained elevated and volatile due to repeated supply shocks from erratic weather patterns [S1].
questions.other_platform_answer: In 2023-24, India's inflation was roughly around 5% to 6%, coming down from higher levels last year. The decline happened because central banks globally raised rates and international commodity prices cooled off, although vegetable prices remained slightly high.

questions.question: What was the policy repo rate and monetary policy stance maintained by the MPC during 2023-24?
contexts: The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) maintained status quo on the policy repo rate at 6.50 per cent throughout 2023-24. The MPC continued with its stance of 'withdrawal of accommodation' to ensure that inflation progressively aligns to the target of 4.0 per cent, while supporting economic growth.
questions.ground_truth: The MPC kept the policy repo rate unchanged at 6.50 per cent throughout 2023-24 and maintained the stance of 'withdrawal of accommodation' to progressively align inflation with the 4.0 per cent target.
questions.policypilot_answer: The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) maintained the policy repo rate at 6.50 per cent throughout 2023-24 [S1]. The committee retained its stance of 'withdrawal of accommodation' to progressively align inflation to the target of 4.0 per cent while supporting growth [S1].
questions.other_platform_answer: The RBI kept the interest rate at 6.5% during the year. They were focusing on bringing down inflation while keeping monetary policy reasonably tight.

questions.question: By how much did the Reserve Bank's balance sheet expand during 2023-24, and what was the final balance sheet size?
contexts: The size of the Reserve Bank's balance sheet increased by ₹6,72,831 crore, i.e., 11.08 per cent, from ₹63,44,756 crore as on March 31, 2023 to ₹70,47,704 crore as on March 31, 2024. The expansion was led by increase in foreign investments, gold reserves, and loans and advances.
questions.ground_truth: The Reserve Bank's balance sheet expanded by ₹6,72,831 crore (11.08 per cent) to reach ₹70,47,704 crore as of March 31, 2024, up from ₹63,44,756 crore in the previous year.
questions.policypilot_answer: The size of the Reserve Bank's balance sheet expanded by ₹6,72,831 crore (11.08 per cent) from ₹63,44,756 crore as on March 31, 2023 to ₹70,47,704 crore as on March 31, 2024 [S1]. The growth was driven by increases in foreign investments, gold reserves, and loans and advances [S1].
questions.other_platform_answer: The RBI balance sheet grew substantially in 2023-24 by over 10% to exceed 70 lakh crore rupees, mainly supported by foreign asset accumulation and domestic lending operations.

contexts: India's foreign exchange reserves stood at US$ 646.4 billion as of March 29, 2024, compared with US$ 578.4 billion a year ago. The reserves provided an import cover of 11.3 months of projected merchandise imports for 2023-24, or 10.6 months of imports of goods and services combined.
questions.ground_truth: India's foreign exchange reserves reached US$ 646.4 billion as of end-March 2024 (up from US$ 578.4 billion), providing an import cover of 11.3 months of merchandise imports.
questions.policypilot_answer: India's foreign exchange reserves stood at US$ 646.4 billion as of March 29, 2024, compared to US$ 578.4 billion a year earlier [S1]. questions.other_platform_answer: India had around 645 billion dollars in forex reserves by March 2024, which was enough to cover about 11 months of imports.

questions.topic: Banking Sector Asset Quality / GNPA Ratio (2023-24)
questions.question: What was the Gross Non-Performing Assets (GNPA) ratio and Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) of Scheduled Commercial Banks at end-March 2024?
contexts: The asset quality of Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs) continued to improve, with the Gross Non-Performing Assets (GNPA) ratio falling to a multi-year low of 2.8 per cent at end-March 2024 from 3.9 per cent at end-March 2023. The Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) of SCBs stood strong at 16.8 per cent at end-March 2024.
questions.ground_truth: Scheduled Commercial Banks achieved a multi-year low GNPA ratio of 2.8 per cent at end-March 2024 (down from 3.9 per cent), while the CRAR stood at a strong 16.8 per cent.
questions.policypilot_answer: The Gross Non-Performing Assets (GNPA) ratio of Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs) fell to a multi-year low of 2.8 per cent at end-March 2024, down from 3.9 per cent in March 2023 [S1]. The Capital to Risk-Weighted Assets Ratio (CRAR) of SCBs remained robust at 16.8 per cent [S1].
questions.other_platform_answer: Indian commercial banks saw their non-performing loans decline to under 3% in 2024, which is the lowest in many years. Their capital adequacy ratio was well above regulatory requirements at around 16%.

questions.question: What was India's Current Account Deficit (CAD) as a percentage of GDP in 2023-24 compared to 2022-23?
contexts: India's current account deficit (CAD) narrowed sharply to US$ 23.2 billion (0.7 per cent of GDP) in 2023-24 from US$ 67.0 billion (2.0 per cent of GDP) in 2022-23. The compression in CAD was supported by lower merchandise trade deficit and robust growth in services exports and remittances.
questions.ground_truth: India's current account deficit narrowed significantly to 0.7 per cent of GDP (US$ 23.2 billion) in 2023-24 from 2.0 per cent of GDP (US$ 67.0 billion) in 2022-23.
questions.policypilot_answer: India's current account deficit (CAD) narrowed sharply to US$ 23.2 billion (0.7 per cent of GDP) in 2023-24 from US$ 67.0 billion (2.0 per cent of GDP) in 2022-23 [S1]. The moderation was driven by a lower merchandise trade deficit and resilient services exports [S1].
questions.other_platform_answer: The current account deficit declined to under 1% of GDP in fiscal 2024, down from 2% in fiscal 2023, largely due to strong software exports.

questions.topic: Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC / e-Rupee) Pilot (2023-24)
questions.question: What progress was made in the pilot implementations of the Central Bank Digital Currency (e₹) during 2023-24?
contexts: During 2023-24, the Reserve Bank expanded the Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) pilots in both wholesale (e₹-W) and retail (e₹-R) segments. The retail pilot (e₹-R) expanded to include over 4.6 million users and 4 lakh merchants across 16 banks in multiple cities. Interoperability with UPI QR codes was introduced in July 2023, significantly boosting merchant acceptance.
questions.ground_truth: The RBI expanded both wholesale and retail CBDC pilots, with e₹-R reaching over 4.6 million users and 4 lakh merchants across 16 banks. UPI QR code interoperability was launched in July 2023.
questions.policypilot_answer: During 2023-24, the Reserve Bank expanded pilots for both wholesale (e₹-W) and retail (e₹-R) CBDC [S1]. The retail pilot (e₹-R) grew to encompass over 4.6 million users and 4 lakh merchants across 16 banks, with UPI QR code interoperability launched in July 2023 to boost acceptance [S1].
questions.other_platform_answer: The RBI continued testing its digital rupee in wholesale and retail formats, adding millions of pilot users and enabling integration with UPI QR codes.

questions.question: What was the overall Priority Sector Lending (PSL) target for commercial banks and did they achieve it in 2023-24?
contexts: All Scheduled Commercial Banks are mandated to achieve an overall Priority Sector Lending (PSL) target of 40 per cent of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC) or Credit Equivalent Amount of Off-Balance Sheet Exposure (CEOBE), whichever is higher. As on March 31, 2024, public and private sector banks collectively achieved an overall PSL achievement ratio of 44.7 per cent.
questions.ground_truth: The mandated PSL target for Scheduled Commercial Banks was 40 per cent of ANBC or CEOBE. As of March 31, 2024, banks achieved an overall PSL ratio of 44.7 per cent.
questions.policypilot_answer: Scheduled Commercial Banks are mandated to meet an overall Priority Sector Lending (PSL) target of 40 per cent of ANBC or CEOBE [S1]. As of March 31, 2024, public and private sector banks achieved an overall PSL achievement ratio of 44.7 per cent [S1].
questions.other_platform_answer: Indian banks are required to lend at least 40% of their net credit to priority sectors including agriculture and small businesses, and they met this target comfortably in 2024.
